strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving repository-level code editing by training on realistic pull request signals rather than relying primarily on complex inference scaffolds. The central idea of converting PRs into verified Search/Replace supervision is well motivated and practically relevant.

The data construction pipeline is described in meaningful detail: filtering of bot/unmerged/non-core PRs, issue linking, reconstruction of before/after states, uniqueness checks for Search/Replace blocks, round-trip verification, repository balancing, and content-based decontamination are all valuable ingredients.

Empirical gains on SWE-bench Lite and Verified are substantial. Clean-PR improves over the base+SFT and StarCoder2-style mid-training baselines, with gains in valid patch rate, file/line localization, and Pass@1. The ablations on Search/Replace format, linked issue context, and error-driven augmentation support the main design choices.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, with useful tables, pipeline diagrams, prompts, training hyperparameters, and dataset statistics. The appendix improves reproducibility relative to many dataset/training papers.
The impact statement acknowledges reliability, security, licensing, and attribution concerns around training on public repositories and deploying code-editing models.
weaknesses: The evidence is still narrower than the claims. The method is evaluated only with Qwen2.5-Coder-32B and primarily on SWE-bench Lite/Verified, so it is unclear whether the proposed mid-training recipe generalizes across model families, model sizes, or multilingual repository-editing benchmarks despite the multilingual dataset claim.

The SFT data raises contamination and attribution questions. The paper uses SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym, and apparently SWE-bench-Live-derived trajectories for Agentless-aligned SFT, but the decontamination discussion is focused mainly on Clean-PR mid-training. More detail is needed to ensure no overlap or near-overlap with SWE-bench Lite/Verified issues, repositories, patches, or derived trajectories leaks through the SFT stage.

Baseline fairness is imperfect. The StarCoder2-style baseline differs from Clean-PR along several axes at once: diff format, filtering, issue augmentation, and possibly retained content distribution. The Python-only ablations help, but the strongest all-language comparison still does not isolate which factors account for the gains.

External comparisons are suggestive but not fully controlled. Results for other open-source systems are copied from original papers and use different scaffolds, decoding strategies, reranking, and possibly evaluation conditions. This weakens claims of state-of-the-art or of outperforming larger systems.

Reproducibility remains limited by scale and release uncertainty. Training requires 32 H200 GPUs for many days, and the paper states that the dataset will be released, but does not provide evidence of code, model checkpoints, exact data snapshots, crawling dates, or scripts sufficient to reproduce the corpus and training end to end.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates or repeated runs. SWE-bench Lite has only 300 instances, so confidence intervals or bootstrap tests would help establish whether some reported differences, especially smaller localization and Pass@1 gains, are robust.

The paper would benefit from deeper error analysis. It reports aggregate valid patch, localization, and pass rates, but does not analyze failure modes such as incorrect issue interpretation, bad file selection, Search/Replace ambiguity, over-editing after augmentation, or security-relevant regressions.

Some claims are overphrased. The model still relies on a structured Agentless scaffold and a dedicated stepwise SFT stage, so the conclusion that repository capabilities are encoded directly into weights and reduce reliance on scaffolding should be stated more cautiously.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: whether repository-level editing ability can be improved through training data rather than increasingly complex agent scaffolds.

The proposed Clean-PR pipeline is conceptually useful: filtering noisy PRs, linking issues, converting diffs to Search/Replace blocks, and round-trip validating patch application are sensible steps for constructing repo-editing supervision.
The scale of the resulting corpus is a real asset if released as described: 2M training PRs across 12 languages with metadata could be valuable to the community.

The experiments include relevant ablations on edit format, issue linking, multilingual data, and error-driven augmentation, and the reported SWE-bench gains over their internal baselines are substantial.
weaknesses: The central claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The paper argues that repo-level capabilities are internalized into model weights and reduce reliance on scaffolding, but evaluation still uses a task-specific Agentless pipeline with file localization, navigation, retrieval constraints, and patch generation prompts.

Contamination control is not convincingly handled for the full training recipe. The appendix describes decontamination for Clean-PR, but the SFT data is derived from SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym, and SWE-bench-Live-like sources, and the paper does not clearly prove that SWE-bench Lite/Verified evaluation instances, gold patches, repositories, or near-duplicates are excluded from SFT trajectories.

The empirical scope is narrow: all main training is on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B and evaluation is essentially SWE-bench Lite/Verified. This makes it hard to know whether the method generalizes across base models, benchmark families, languages, or real development workflows.

The baseline comparisons are not fully fair or sufficiently controlled. External results are copied from prior papers with different inference frameworks and model/training details, while the StarCoder2-style baseline differs along several axes beyond data format, including filtering, issue context, and sampling.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper promises dataset release, but does not provide enough detail to reproduce the GitHub crawl, exact filtering decisions, SFT source splits, contamination checks, or evaluation harness. The required compute is also very high.

Several important analyses are missing: manual quality estimates of Clean-PR examples, license/attribution filtering outcomes, failure analysis on SWE-bench, statistical uncertainty over benchmark scores, and whether improvements come from mid-training versus exposure to SWE-style SFT data.

Presentation has inconsistencies and overstatements, e.g. the text reports a Base+SFT Lite score of 10.3 while Table 6 shows 11.3, and claims of state-of-the-art or superiority over larger models are not well supported by apples-to-apples comparisons.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: whether repository-level editing ability can be internalized through training rather than mainly obtained through heavy agent scaffolding. A 2M-instance PR-derived Search/Replace corpus with issue augmentation would be a useful resource if released as described.

Soundness: The data pipeline is thoughtfully engineered. The paper gives concrete filtering, issue-linking, Search/Replace conversion, round-trip verification, complexity control, repository sampling, and decontamination procedures. These choices are well motivated for reducing noise in raw GitHub PRs.

Empirical results are promising. Clean-PR improves substantially over the Qwen2.5-Coder-32B baselines on SWE-bench Lite and Verified, including gains over a StarCoder2-style PR baseline of similar token scale. The ablations on Search/Replace format, linked issues, and error-driven SFT support the main design choices.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear, with useful tables for dataset construction, training setup, language distribution, prompts, and baseline construction. The appendix contains enough procedural detail to make the pipeline understandable.

Originality: The main novelty is not a new model architecture but a large-scale, validated PR-to-repository-edit training signal. The combination of verified Search/Replace supervision, linked issue context, and Agentless-aligned SFT is a meaningful and practically relevant contribution.
weaknesses: The causal attribution is not fully isolated. The strongest model differs from baselines along several axes: filtering, linked issues, Search/Replace format, language mix, SFT data, and error-driven augmentation. The paper includes useful ablations, but mostly on the Python subset and not a full factorial comparison at the final scale.

The evaluation is narrow relative to the claims. The main results are on SWE-bench Lite and Verified, both Python-centric and closely aligned with the Agentless workflow. The paper claims broad repository-level capability across 12 languages, but does not evaluate on multilingual repo-level benchmarks or substantially different software-engineering tasks.

Generalization across base models is untested. All main experiments use Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, so it is unclear whether the training recipe transfers to smaller models, different model families, or stronger recent bases.

The comparison to external systems is only partially convincing. The paper compares against open-source agentic or larger-model methods, but differences in framework, decoding, retrieval, benchmark protocol, and reporting make these results more contextual than definitive evidence of superiority.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete. The paper provides many implementation details and says the dataset will be released, but acceptance would depend on actual availability of the data, code, scripts, exact splits, model checkpoints, and decontamination artifacts. The compute requirement is also very high, limiting independent reproduction.

The treatment of licensing and ethics is brief. The impact statement acknowledges public-repository licensing, attribution, security, and misuse concerns, but does not specify concrete license filtering for Clean-PR itself, attribution mechanics, opt-out handling, or safeguards for training on potentially sensitive public code.

Some claims are overstated. Phrases such as proving repository-level capability can be encoded into weights or reducing reliance on heavy scaffolding are directionally supported, but the method still uses a structured Agentless scaffold and the absolute SWE-bench scores remain moderate. I would soften these claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in repository-level code editing: whether useful SWE capabilities can be internalized through training data rather than mainly obtained through complex inference scaffolding.

The Clean-PR data pipeline is a substantial contribution. It starts from 16.4M GitHub PRs, applies explicit filtering, issue linking, Search/Replace conversion, round-trip validation, repository balancing, and contamination controls, yielding a large 2M-instance / 17.7B-token training corpus.

The empirical evaluation is convincing overall. On SWE-bench Lite and Verified, Clean-PR gives large gains over Qwen2.5-Coder baselines, SFT-only models, and a StarCoder2-style PR-data baseline, with useful intermediate metrics for valid patch rate, file localization, and line localization.
The ablations are well targeted: edit format, linked issue context, multilingual training, and error-driven augmentation are each studied, making the central data-design choices more credible.

The paper goes beyond one benchmark setting by including 7B scale transfer, Multi-SWE-bench Flash multilingual evaluation, OpenHands agentic evaluation, and general coding benchmarks to check catastrophic forgetting.
Presentation is generally clear, with good tables, a readable pipeline diagram, detailed prompts, training hyperparameters, and an appendix describing filtering, formatting, and decontamination.
weaknesses: The contribution is mostly data engineering and training recipe design rather than a fundamentally new learning method. The core ingredients, such as PR mining, Search/Replace edits, Agentless-style decomposition, and hard-negative augmentation, are individually familiar; the originality lies mainly in scale and integration.

Reproducibility is limited by cost and release uncertainty. The paper states that it plans to release the dataset, but the full crawl, filtering pipeline, training recipe, and 32-H200 multi-stage training are expensive and may be difficult for others to independently reproduce.

The comparison to external systems is somewhat incomplete. The paper emphasizes reduced inference scaffolding, but Table 7 uses a small set of open-source baselines and does not deeply normalize for inference budget, retrieval setup, benchmark date, verifier usage, or newer high-performing agentic systems.

The dataset quality claims depend heavily on heuristic filters. Bot detection, title/description blocklists, issue-linking regexes, extension-based language purity, and exclusion of broad PRs may introduce selection bias toward simple or conventional fixes, and the paper only lightly analyzes what useful edits are lost.

The decontamination discussion is stronger than many papers but still cannot fully rule out semantic leakage from public GitHub code, forks, vendored code, or common issue/fix patterns. The similarity-quintile analysis is reassuring but not decisive.

The method under-represents large, cross-cutting repository changes by construction, with an at-most-five-core-files filter and windowing around edit spans. This limits the claim that the model internalizes general repository-level engineering rather than relatively localized repair behavior.

Ethics and limitations are present but brief. The impact statement notes licensing, attribution, reliability, and malicious automation risks, but there is little concrete discussion of privacy in PR text/comments, security evaluation of generated patches, or dataset governance for opt-outs and takedown requests.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: improving repository-level code editing by training on PR-scale supervision rather than relying only on heavier inference-time agent scaffolding.

The proposed data pipeline is plausible and reasonably detailed: filtering noisy PRs, linking issues, converting diffs to Search/Replace blocks, and round-trip validation are all sensible design choices for repo-level editing supervision.

The empirical results show consistent gains over internal baselines on SWE-bench Lite and Verified, with additional ablations for edit format, issue linking, error-driven augmentation, 7B scaling, multilingual evaluation, and OpenHands transfer.
The paper includes useful decontamination discussion, including repository exclusion, file hashing, n-gram overlap filtering, issue similarity filtering, and a nearest-neighbor leakage analysis.
weaknesses: The central claim that repository-level capabilities are internalized into model weights is overstated. The final system still depends on an Agentless-style decomposition, SFT on SWE-style trajectories, retrieval/top-3 file constraints, and Search/Replace-specific prompting. The evidence does not cleanly separate model-internal capability from scaffold alignment and benchmark-specific supervision.

The evaluation is not strong enough for the breadth of the claims. Comparisons to external methods are copied from original papers rather than reproduced under matched inference budgets, decoding settings, model families, or scaffolds. The strongest comparisons are therefore not fully controlled.

The ablations are helpful but incomplete. The paper does not isolate all major factors in the full 17.7B-token setting, such as filtering, issue linking, Search/Replace conversion, repository sampling, and SFT augmentation independently. The StarCoder2-style baseline differs in several ways at once, making attribution uncertain.

Reproducibility is limited. Training requires 32 H200 GPUs for hundreds of hours, and the paper says the dataset will be released rather than clearly providing an available artifact, code, exact crawling snapshot, scripts, and trained checkpoints. Without these, the main contribution is hard for others to verify or build on.

The data ethics and licensing treatment is too shallow for a large-scale GitHub corpus. The impact statement acknowledges licensing and attribution but does not clearly specify license filtering for Clean-PR itself, opt-out handling, redistribution constraints, privacy/PII processing, or whether linked issue and comment text can be redistributed safely.

The reported gains on SWE-bench are meaningful but not exceptional in absolute terms, and the multilingual result remains low at 12.3% Pass@1. This weakens the significance claim that the method broadly solves repository-level editing beyond the specific Python SWE-bench setting.

There are presentation and precision issues: some tables are visually cramped or malformed in extraction, terminology such as 'largest publicly released' conflicts with 'we plan to release,' and several causal explanations are phrased speculatively while being presented as strong conclusions.

The paper lacks uncertainty estimates, multiple random seeds, or statistical testing for the main benchmark gains. Given the small benchmark sizes and stochastic training/sampling choices, this makes it harder to assess robustness.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: improving repository-level code editing by shifting capability into model weights rather than relying mainly on complex inference scaffolds. The central idea of mining accepted pull requests into verified Search/Replace training instances is well motivated and useful.

The proposed Clean-PR pipeline is technically thoughtful. The paper describes filtering, issue linking, reconstruction of before/after states, minimal unique Search/Replace conversion, and round-trip verification. These steps directly target known sources of noise in raw GitHub PR data.

The empirical evaluation is broad and mostly convincing. The main SWE-bench Lite and Verified results show large gains over Qwen2.5-Coder baselines, and the paper includes controlled comparisons to a StarCoder2-style PR baseline with similar token budget.

Ablations support several key design choices: Search/Replace format outperforms diffs, linked issue context helps, error-driven SFT augmentation improves Pass@1 and line localization, and the method transfers to a 7B model, multilingual repair, and an OpenHands agentic setup.
The dataset scale is significant: 2M training PRs across 12 languages and 17.7B tokens after filtering. If released as promised with metadata, this would be a valuable resource for the community.

The paper makes a reasonable effort to address contamination, including repository exclusion, file hashing, n-gram overlap, issue similarity filtering, and a semantic leakage analysis over SWE-bench Verified.
weaknesses: The evidence does not fully isolate all parts of the data pipeline. The StarCoder2-style baseline differs in format, filtering, retained file types, and issue augmentation, while the cleaner ablations are mainly on the Python subset. This leaves some uncertainty about which components are essential at full scale.

The central claim that repository-level ability is internalized into weights is plausible but somewhat overstated. The final system still depends on an Agentless-style decomposition, retrieval/localization prompts, and SFT trajectories from SWE-oriented datasets; the experiments show reduced scaffolding rather than scaffolding-free repair ability.

Reproducibility remains partly contingent on future release. The paper says it plans to release the dataset and gives useful schema/training details, but it is unclear whether code, exact data snapshots, filtering scripts, model checkpoints, and evaluation scripts will be available. Reproducing 259 hours of 32B training on 32 H200s is also costly.

The treatment of possible overlap and contamination in the SFT data could be clearer. Clean-PR decontamination is described in detail, but the Agentless-aligned SFT sources include SWE-rebench and SWE-Gym; the paper should more explicitly state task/repository overlap controls relative to SWE-bench Lite/Verified and Multi-SWE-bench evaluations.

External comparisons are useful but not fully controlled. Some results are copied from original papers and use different frameworks, model sizes, decoding budgets, or evaluation conditions. The paper should be more cautious in claiming state-of-the-art superiority over systems with different inference protocols.

The ethical and legal discussion is relatively brief for a large-scale GitHub-derived dataset. Licensing, attribution, opt-outs, personal data in issues/comments, and security risks are acknowledged but not operationalized in much detail beyond the impact statement and release schema.

The limitations section is honest but short. It notes under-representation of broad cross-cutting PRs and untested model families, but says little about failure modes by issue category, repository size, test availability, security-sensitive edits, or how often generated Search/Replace patches are semantically wrong despite applying cleanly.
